title: What’s the Deal with Student Motivation? Or: On the Teaching of Souls
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: In the opening piece of his student-motivation series, Dave Stuart Jr. argues that education suffers from foggy thinking about what students are and what schools are for. He traces a drift from treating students as brains on sticks, through the brain-science fad, to an expansive social-emotional learning movement, none of it answering the basic questions of what a person is and what a teacher's job is. Drawing on Dallas Willard, he describes a person as a five-part soul: intellectual, emotional, physical, social and volitional. Using a relay-race image, he says flourishing is a group project in which many adults take part, and that the school's distinctive lane is developing the mind through mastery of the disciplines and arts. He is explicit that this does not license ignoring social and emotional growth, and he ends by previewing the claim that the heart is the best path to the head.
points: Stuart diagnoses a pattern in which education chases one lens after another (brains, then SEL) without a settled view of what a student is.
He adopts Dallas Willard's five-part account of the person as intellectual, emotional, physical, social and volitional.
The relay-race metaphor casts long-term flourishing as a shared project and gives schools the mind as their unique lane.
He guards the claim by insisting that focusing on the mind does not mean neglecting social and emotional development.
The post sets up the follow-on argument that motivation work through the heart is the best route to academic learning.
quotes: The trouble was just that we got to this place where there was an unspoken sense that people are brains on sticks. It was myopia — near-sightedness. We lost the forest for the trees.
But again — there is all kinds of goodness in seeking the social and emotional maturation of a human being. I want such maturity for my own children. I want it for myself.

My trouble with it all is only this: I’m unclear on some basic questions. What’s a person? What’s my job? Where can I make my largest contribution as a teacher of young people in a public high school?

What’s important for our purposes is this old-fashioned, cross-cultural idea that people are mostly invisible creatures comprised of five parts. We’re not just the bodies you see but are very much comprised of intellect, emotion, will, and relationship. Development in these five areas is what promotes the long-term flourishing of a person.

Now, I’m not giving license here to ignore SEL — by all means, seek the social and emotional development of the young people in your care. Nor am I saying that the mind is just the brain — I think it’s more than that. I’m just saying, the mind is our spot.

Of course it isn’t! And a 400×4 relay isn’t all about the second lap. Nonetheless, the second runner must run their race, striving for excellence in it alone, seeking to eke every last bit of performance they can from it for the sake of the goal.
